speaker: Matei Zaharia
title: The Agent Cloud: Databricks' Bet on the Future of AI — Matei Zaharia and Reynold Xin
question: In data and AI infrastructure, what determines which layers of a platform should be open-sourced versus kept as a proprietary commercial offering?
guest: One reason to open source something is if it is a layer that will have a network effect and benefit from many people collaborating on it. With Spark, there used to be separate distributed computing engines for machine learning and graph computation, and we said they should all be composable libraries and made it super easy to add connectors to data sources. We benefit because we do not have time to write connectors to a thousand different databases and file formats, so we use the ones people make and they benefit from joining. Another way to think about it: imagine our agent hosting layer was not open, and there was an open one—which one wins in the long run? Because of the benefit from people writing integrations, the open one wins. Then there are other things you cannot even deliver as open source, like making sure your streaming jobs or database do not lose all your data at night. That requires an operational team sitting there; it has to be a service. So we want to be really good at those infrastructure services and as open as we can on what you build on top.

points.core: Open-source layers where ecosystem network effects make external integrations indispensable.
points.note: Accept: open-sourcing components that gain value from many contributors building composable libraries or integrations. Do not credit: generic claims that open source builds community goodwill or developer adoption.

points.core: No single vendor can maintain connectors for thousands of external data systems alone.
points.note: Accept: third-party contributors writing adapters for diverse databases, file formats, or harnesses that the vendor lacks bandwidth to build. Do not credit: vague statements that open source saves engineering time.

points.core: Closed integration layers lose long-term whenever a credible open alternative attracts external contributors.
points.note: Accept: competitive counterfactual showing an open-source standard outcompetes a closed equivalent when third-party integrations drive value. Do not credit: generic assertions that open source always beats proprietary software.

points.core: Operational reliability that prevents overnight data loss requires a dedicated managed service team.
points.note: Accept: commercializing hosted infrastructure operations, uptime guarantees, or database/streaming reliability that cannot be shipped as open-source code alone. Do not credit: generic claims about selling enterprise support or SLAs without the code-vs-operations distinction.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The dividing line is usually set by where adoption and trust matter most versus where differentiated, hard-to-replicate value sits.

Layers that benefit from being standards tend to be opened: file and table formats, APIs, query engines, frameworks and client libraries. Openness there drives adoption, builds an ecosystem of integrations and contributors, and reassures buyers they are not locked in, since their data and code remain portable. These layers also tend to commoditize anyway, so keeping them closed yields little advantage.

Layers that tend to stay proprietary are those where value comes from operating the software rather than from the code itself: the managed control plane, performance optimizations, autoscaling, and enterprise features such as security, governance, compliance, and support. A common heuristic is that features an individual developer needs are open, while features an organization's management needs are paid.

Competitive dynamics shape the line too. The risk of cloud providers reselling the project as a service pushes vendors toward restrictive licences or closed operational layers, while a challenger may open-source a layer specifically to commoditize a rival's advantage. Databricks, Confluent and Snowflake's moves around Delta Lake, Kafka and Iceberg illustrate each pattern.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
In data and AI infrastructure, the boundary between open-source and proprietary layers is determined by separating what drives developer adoption from what enterprises pay to operate at scale. Vendors typically open-source foundational layers—such as data formats, core runtimes, SDKs, and APIs—because engineers strongly resist vendor lock-in around their data and code. Openness at this layer builds trust, removes friction for bottom-up adoption, and encourages ecosystem integrations that can turn a project into an industry standard.

Conversely, capabilities addressing organizational complexity, operational toil, and risk remain proprietary. When workloads move from individual experimentation to mission-critical production, the buyer shifts from a practitioner to an executive focused on reliability, security, and total cost of ownership. Vendors therefore monetize the control plane and enterprise features: managed cloud orchestration, autoscaling, specialized performance accelerators, multi-tenancy, fine-grained access controls, data lineage, and compliance auditing. Simply put, successful platforms open-source the primitives for building and commercialize the machinery for governing and scaling across an organization.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The usual dividing line is who gets the value from a layer and where the cost of running it lands. Companies tend to open-source the layers that benefit from wide adoption, community contributions, and trust. These are things like file and table formats (Parquet, Iceberg, Delta), query engines, SDKs, model weights, and APIs, where being open becomes the standard. Developers adopt these from the bottom up, and the lock-in worries that slow enterprise buying go away.

What stays proprietary is the work enterprises will pay to avoid doing themselves. That includes managed hosting and operations, elastic scaling, security, governance, compliance, access control, multi-tenant management, observability, and service-level guarantees. This "open core" or "open source, sell the cloud" model works because that value grows with organizational complexity, not with how many individual developers use the tool.

A few other factors shape the line. Hyperscalers can host your open project and compete with you, which pushed companies like Elastic, MongoDB, and HashiCorp toward restrictive licenses. Openness also brings ecosystem network effects. A company has to decide whether its edge comes from the code itself or from running it. And if a layer is becoming a commodity anyway, opening it early can let you set the standard.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon

In data and AI infrastructure, the boundary between open-source and proprietary layers is primarily determined by where ecosystem adoption creates leverage versus where enterprise operational complexity drives willingness to pay.

Platforms typically open-source foundational primitives—such as file and table formats, query or inference engines, SDKs, and core protocols—because openness lowers adoption friction, eases vendor lock-in concerns, attracts community integrations, and helps establish de facto industry standards. Bottom-up developer adoption depends on transparency, portability, and ease of local experimentation.

Conversely, vendors keep layers proprietary when they address organizational scale, reliability, and risk rather than individual developer utility. Managed control planes, automated scaling and cost optimization, multi-tenant isolation, fine-grained security, governance, compliance auditing, and enterprise observability are expensive to build and operate, making enterprises willing to pay for them. Proprietary layers also defend against cloud hyperscalers commoditizing open-source engines by anchoring commercial value in managed performance, workflow orchestration, and production-grade SLAs.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Open-source the layers where broad adoption, interoperability, and community contributions create the most value. In data and AI infrastructure, that often means file formats, APIs, connectors, and sometimes the core engine. Opening those layers makes the platform easier to adopt, integrate, and build on.

Keep a layer proprietary when it delivers differentiated value customers will pay for and opening it would do little to grow the ecosystem. That could be a managed service that handles scaling, upgrades, and uptime, or enterprise features such as centralized governance. The boundary depends on where the platform can sustain a competitive advantage. If customers pay for reliable operations, the engine can be open. If they pay for a substantial performance advantage built into the engine, there’s a stronger case for keeping that part proprietary.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The choice depends on where openness increases adoption and trust, and where customers will pay for a distinct advantage. Open-sourcing a file format, API implementation, or processing engine can make a platform easier to evaluate, integrate, and build on. That’s especially valuable when the layer becomes more useful as other tools adopt it, or when customers need assurance that they can move their data and workloads elsewhere.

A commercial offering makes sense where the vendor delivers measurable value customers would find costly to reproduce, such as operating an open engine reliably at scale, optimizing it for particular workloads, or providing enterprise governance and support. A core algorithm can also stay proprietary if its performance is what customers buy. A practical test is to ask what opening a layer would help users and partners do, and what they would still pay the vendor to do better.
